body:
Why must an invention be described in writing?

A patent application does more than identify the inventor. It must explain the claimed invention so that its technical subject matter can be understood and evaluated. This written disclosure is called the patent specification.

The specification has 2 related functions. It provides technical information about the invention, and the claims in a complete specification identify the legal scope of protection being requested.

Provisional and complete specifications

Under Section 9 of the Patents Act, 1970, an eligible Indian patent application may be filed with a provisional specification or directly with a complete specification.

Provisional specification

A provisional specification describes an invention at an early stage and can establish a filing date for the material adequately disclosed in it. It is useful when an inventor has developed a sufficiently definite invention but has not completed every aspect of the final specification.

A provisional specification does not itself result in the grant of a patent. Where an application is initially filed with a provisional specification under Section 9(1), the complete specification must be filed within 12 months of the application filing date. Otherwise, the application is deemed abandoned. The ordinary 12-month period cannot be extended for this purpose.

Complete specification

A complete specification contains the full legally required disclosure and the claims defining the invention for which patent protection is sought. Its content is governed principally by Section 10.

FeatureProvisional specificationComplete specification
Principal purposeDisclose the invention and establish a priority date for claims adequately supported by itProvide full disclosure and define the protection sought
DescriptionDescribes the invention sufficiently to support the relevant disclosureFully and particularly describes the invention and its operation or use
ClaimsNot ordinarily requiredRequired to define the scope of protection
Relationship to grantMust ordinarily be followed by a complete specification within 12 monthsForms the basis for substantive examination and possible grant

Contents of a complete specification

Section 10 requires a complete specification to contain sufficient information about the invention. The principal elements are:

  • Title: identifies the subject matter of the invention.
  • Full description: explains the invention, its operation or use, and the method by which it is to be performed.
  • Best known method: discloses the best method of performing the invention known to the applicant and for which protection is claimed.
  • Claims: define the scope of the invention for which protection is sought.
  • Abstract: provides concise technical information about the invention.
  • Drawings: may support the explanation and must be supplied when required by the Controller.

The claims must be clear, succinct and fairly based on the matter disclosed in the specification. They must relate to a single invention or a group of inventions linked by a single inventive concept.

Why are patent claims so important?

The claims mark the legal boundary of the protection sought and, if granted, the protection conferred. The description explains how the invention works, while the claims identify the technical features covered by the exclusive right.

Suppose an inventor develops a particular automatic valve mechanism. The description may explain the problem of water leakage, the components of the valve, how they interact and how the mechanism operates. A claim would identify the combination of technical features for which the inventor seeks protection.

Not every feature mentioned in the description is automatically protected as an independent monopoly. The scope depends on the granted claims, interpreted according to patent law.

Broad idea versus technical claim

The statement a device that prevents water wastage expresses a desired result. It does not clearly identify the technical features of a particular invention. A properly drafted patent claim must define the relevant technical subject matter rather than merely state the benefit the inventor hopes to achieve.

Disclosure and the public interest

The disclosure requirement prevents an applicant from demanding broad exclusive protection while concealing how the claimed invention is carried out. Sufficient disclosure also enables examiners and other interested persons to assess whether the claimed invention deserves a patent.

For inventions involving certain biological materials, Section 10 contains additional requirements concerning disclosure, including the source and geographical origin of biological material used in the invention.

Prelims focus

  • Section 9 governs provisional and complete specifications.
  • A complete specification must ordinarily be filed within 12 months after a provisional filing under Section 9(1).
  • Section 10 governs the contents of specifications.
  • The description explains the invention; the claims define the scope of protection.
  • The abstract supplies technical information and does not replace the claims.
  • Trap: Filing a provisional specification does not mean that a patent has already been granted.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 9 and 10, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Filing Process, provisions concerning provisional and complete specifications (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Manual of Patent Office Practice and Procedure, Section 05.02, Provisional Specification.]

title: Patent Specifications, Claims and Disclosure of an Invention

body:
Which authority grants Indian patents?

Patent applications are examined through the Indian Patent Office, which functions under the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks. The Controller of Patents exercises the statutory powers involved in examining applications, considering objections and granting or refusing patents.

A person does not receive a patent merely by submitting an application or paying a filing fee. A grant follows the prescribed procedure and depends on compliance with the law.

Who may apply?

Section 6 permits an application to be made by the person claiming to be the true and first inventor, an assignee deriving the right to apply from that person, or the legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled to apply.

An inventor is the person responsible for the invention. An applicant is the person or entity legally seeking the patent. They may be the same person, but they need not be. For example, an organisation may apply as an assignee when the relevant rights have lawfully been transferred to it.

Main stages of the patent procedure

1. Filing the application

The applicant files the prescribed documents and fees, including the specification. An eligible application may begin with a provisional specification or be filed directly with a complete specification. Indian patent applications can be filed electronically through the Patent Office system.

When a provisional specification is filed under Section 9(1), a complete specification must follow within 12 months. Filing establishes a filing date; it does not guarantee novelty, validity or grant.

2. Publication of the application

Under Section 11A and Rule 24, a patent application is ordinarily published after 18 months from the filing date or priority date, whichever is earlier. The applicant may request early publication. Certain applications, such as those subject to secrecy directions or qualifying abandoned or withdrawn applications, are exceptions to ordinary publication.

Publication makes specified information about the application publicly available. It is different from the publication of a granted patent.

3. Request for examination

Examination is not automatic merely because an application has been filed or published. A prescribed request for examination is required under Section 11B. The ordinary request is made using Form 18.

Under Rule 24B as amended in 2024, the normal deadline for requesting examination is 31 months from the earlier of the relevant filing and priority dates for applications filed on or after commencement of the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024, on 15 March 2024. For applications filed before that commencement, the earlier applicable time limit of 48 months is preserved. Specific categories of applications have additional rules.

Publication and the request for examination should not be imagined as steps that must always occur one after the other. An examination request may be submitted before publication; substantive processing follows the applicable statutory procedure.

4. Examination and objections

The Patent Office examines whether the application satisfies patentability requirements, including novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, eligibility and the adequacy of the specification.

If objections arise, the Controller communicates them to the applicant, commonly through a First Examination Report (FER). The applicant may respond with explanations and permissible amendments.

Rule 24B ordinarily provides 6 months from issuance of the first statement of objections to put the application in order for grant, with a specified extension of 3 months available through a timely request in Form 4. Rule 138 permits the Controller to extend time or condone delay under the Rules by up to 6 months on a request in Form 4 made before that 6-month period expires; relief is discretionary.

5. Grant or refusal

If the application meets the legal requirements and any opposition issues are resolved, the Controller may grant the patent under Section 43. The grant is published, and the patent becomes subject to the statutory rights, conditions and renewal requirements.

If the objections are not overcome or the invention is not legally patentable, the Controller may refuse the application in accordance with the Act.

Does a published application give the same protection as a granted patent?

No. Section 11A(7) provides certain privileges and rights from publication of an application, subject to statutory conditions. However, the applicant cannot institute infringement proceedings until the patent has been granted.

Thus, the distinction among application filed, application published and patent granted is essential. These are different legal stages.

Dates must not be confused

The 12-month period relates to filing a complete specification after a provisional application. The usual 18-month period concerns publication. The examination-request deadline is generally 31 months for applications governed by the 2024 amendment. None of these periods is the patent term, which is normally 20 years from filing.

Prelims focus

  • Section 11A deals with publication of patent applications; ordinary publication occurs after 18 months from filing or priority, whichever is earlier.
  • Section 11B requires a request for examination; the ordinary request uses Form 18.
  • Rule 24B provides a 31-month examination-request deadline for applications governed by the 2024 amendment.
  • The earlier 48-month deadline is preserved for applications filed before 15 March 2024.
  • A First Examination Report communicates examination objections.
  • Trap: Publication of an application is not the grant of a patent.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 6, 7, 9, 11A, 11B, 12–15, 21 and 43, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); The Patents Rules, 2003, Rules 24 and 24B, as amended by the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024, effective 15 March 2024 (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Filing Process and Frequently Asked Questions on Patents, sections on filing, examination and grant (consulted 14 November 2026). Procedural status and deadlines stated as applicable at the content cutoff of 14 November 2026.]

title: Filing, Publication, Examination and Grant of an Indian Patent

body:
Why does patent law allow opposition?

Patent examination is intended to prevent the grant of invalid patents. However, other persons may possess information that an examiner has not identified. For example, a researcher may know of an earlier publication, or a community may possess traditional knowledge relevant to the claimed invention.

The opposition procedure enables eligible persons to present specified legal grounds against a patent application or an already granted patent. Section 25 of the Patents Act, 1970, provides for pre-grant opposition and post-grant opposition.

Pre-grant opposition

A pre-grant opposition may be made after the patent application has been published but before the patent is granted. Under Section 25(1), any person may submit a representation by way of opposition to the Controller on the grounds permitted by law.

For example, a person may produce an earlier technical publication showing that the claimed invention was already known. Other permitted grounds include wrongful obtaining of the invention, specified prior use or claiming, lack of inventive step, lack of patentability, insufficient disclosure, and relevant traditional or indigenous knowledge.

The representation is filed in Form 7A with a statement, supporting evidence if any, and an optional request for a hearing; the Controller considers it only after examination has been requested. The Controller may reject an unsubstantiated objection or take appropriate action where the legal requirements are not satisfied.

Post-grant opposition

A post-grant opposition challenges a patent after grant. Under Section 25(2), it may be initiated by any person interested within 1 year from the date of publication of the grant of the patent.

A person interested is not necessarily the inventor. The expression includes persons with a legally relevant interest in the invention, such as those engaged in or promoting research in the relevant technical field or having a relevant commercial interest.

In post-grant opposition, an Opposition Board examines the case and makes its recommendation. After considering the proceedings, the Controller may maintain the patent, require appropriate amendments or revoke it in accordance with the law.

Common grounds of opposition

Opposition is available only on the grounds specified by Section 25. Important examples include:

  • Wrongful obtaining: the applicant or patentee improperly obtained the invention from another person.
  • Prior publication or other anticipation: the invention was already disclosed in a legally relevant manner before the claim's priority date.
  • Obviousness: the invention lacks an inventive step.
  • Non-patentable subject matter: the claim falls within a statutory exclusion.
  • Insufficient description: the complete specification does not adequately describe the invention or the method of performing it.
  • Traditional knowledge: the claim is anticipated by relevant knowledge, including oral knowledge, available within a local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere.

These examples show why a complete and accurate specification matters. A patent application can fail not only because the technology was previously known but also because the claimed invention has not been sufficiently disclosed.

The role of the Controller

The Controller exercises the powers assigned by the Patents Act and Rules. In a post-grant opposition, the statutory process includes an Opposition Board and an opportunity for the parties to be heard as applicable.

Indian law also requires that an application not be granted before 6 months have passed after its publication. This allows an initial opportunity for pre-grant opposition. It does not mean that every application must be granted after 6 months.

Opposition is different from infringement

Opposition concerns whether a patent should be granted or remain valid. Infringement concerns whether someone has carried out an act prohibited by an enforceable patent without legal justification.

Thus, a person questioning the novelty of a granted patent raises a validity issue. A patent holder alleging that a competitor is manufacturing a product covered by valid patent claims raises an infringement issue.

Prelims focus

  • Section 25 governs pre-grant and post-grant opposition.
  • Pre-grant opposition may be initiated by any person after application publication and before grant.
  • Post-grant opposition may be initiated by a person interested.
  • The ordinary post-grant opposition period is 1 year from publication of the patent grant.
  • An Opposition Board participates in post-grant opposition proceedings.
  • Trap: The 1-year period for post-grant opposition is not counted from the original filing date.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Section 25, including subsections 25(1) and 25(2), Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); The Patents Rules, 2003, Rule 55 and related opposition provisions, as amended (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Frequently Asked Questions on Patents, questions concerning pre-grant and post-grant opposition (consulted 14 November 2026).]
